name: OK Computer
description_preview:
Despite not having a hit anywhere near the size of “Creep”, Radiohead’s previous album The Bends (1995) was successful enough for their record company EMI to give them complete creative control. The result was 1997’s OK Computer, which was designed as a deliberate reaction against the grunge movement of the 1990s. Then new-ish engineer and future Radiohead mainstay Nigel Godrich told Rolling Stone of the recording sessions:

They were the band of my dreams. There were no constraints. This was not Neanderthal rock & roll. It was very high-level thinking, conceptual, moving forwards in terms of sonics, and beautiful songs. It was a perfect thing. Lots of people, lots of ideas, and we all could pull in the same direction.

The album’s lyrical themes and composition have it hailed as way ahead of its time, predictive of society’s obsession with technology, and the isolation and paranoia that comes with it. Yorke, however, explained that it stemmed mostly from his personal experiences travelling non-stop in a touring band.

The paranoia I felt at the time was much more related to how people related to each other. But I was using the terminology of technology to express it. Everything I was writing was actually a way of trying to reconnect with other human beings when you’re always in transit. That’s what I had to write about because that’s what was going on, which in itself instilled a kind of loneliness and disconnection.

OK Computer was released to universal acclaim upon its release, and is often considered to be one of the greatest albums of all time. On its twentieth anniversary in 2017, the band released a deluxe set including B-sides and never-before-released studio versions of songs, titled OK COMPUTER OKNOTOK 1997 2017.

description_annotation.twitter_share_message: “The cover art for OK Computer is a digital collage of several images, and was designed by frontm…” —@Genius

body.plain:
The cover art for OK Computer is a digital collage of several images, and was designed by frontman Thom Yorke and longtime collaborator Stanley Donwood. Donwood recalled the creation process in a 2010 Pitchfork interview:

I remember we were trying to make something the colour of bleached bone. We had a rule that if we made a mistake we had to scribble over it — we couldn’t do the Apple-Z thing, we couldn’t undo. It was done on an early Apple Mac.

He further describes the intended aesthetic in this interview, saying:

I wanted to just create a kind of fog world. There were lots of fragments of images and found stuff, things I just found on the street that I scanned into a computer along with bits of text. One was an airplane-safety guide Thom stole from a commercial flight.

The repeated words “Lost Child” in the top right are taken from airport signs, resembling the theme of alienation that the album explores. Following the release of Donwood’s concept art in 2017 alongside the album’s twentieth anniversary reissue, the location of the highway in the image was discovered by a Reddit user.

description_annotation.twitter_share_message: “This is the image that appears on the back of the CD cover booklet. Radiohead’s notoriously spec…” —@Genius

body.plain:
This is the image that appears on the back of the CD cover booklet. Radiohead’s notoriously speculative fanbase have noticed that, if you look closely just under the picture of the tree, you can see words “Street Spirit” faintly handwritten, which is reference to the band’s 1995 hit single of the same name.

Beneath the words “plane surface” is the album’s track list, but between “No Surprises” and “Lucky” there is a big gap. This has led to speculation that the songs “A Reminder” and “Polyethylene”, which both nearly made it onto OK Computer and later appeared as B-sides, were originally meant to fill this gap but were cut last-minute.

body.plain:
Used twice on the artwork, once in the booklet and once on the CD itself, is the image of two stick figures shaking hands, which would later appear on the band’s The Best Of compilation.

Yorke explained the picture as symbolising exploitation, saying:

Someone’s being sold something they don’t really want, and someone’s being friendly because they’re trying to sell something. That’s what it means to me."

The image bears similarity to the cover of Pink Floyd’s Wish You Were Here, an album that deals with exploitation in the music business.

description_annotation.twitter_share_message: “OK Computer’s artwork is a collage of pictures and text created by Stanley Donwood and Thom York…” —@Genius

body.plain:
OK Computer’s artwork is a collage of pictures and text created by Stanley Donwood and Thom Yorke.

The colour palette is predominantly white and blue, according to Stanley, the result of “trying to make something the color of bleached bone”. This approach attempted to subvert black as a color of death, replacing it with a bright white. Donwood explained,

I got the completely mistaken idea that white was somehow the color of death, so I wanted it white. I know it’s usually black, but I was thinking it was some other culture where white is the color of death. I was quite a morbid character.”

Explaining the artwork’s themes, Yorke said:

It’s quite sad, and quite funny as well. All the artwork and so on … It was all the things that I hadn’t said in the songs."

Motifs in the art include motorways, aeroplanes, families with children, corporate logos and cityscapes. The non-sequiturs created an effect akin to being lifestyle-coached by a lunatic. White scribbles, Donwood’s method of correcting mistakes rather than using the computer function undo, are present everywhere in the collages.

The back cover of the album features a tridimensional map of an underground rail-road platform. The origin of the map is unclear. Perhaps it could also be from some metro station in Prague?

Beneath the tracklist are the words “we hope that you choke”, which are taken from the song “Exit Music (For a Film)”. The long number, 18576397, refers to the exact time the album was finished, at 18:57 on the 6th of March (3) 1997
